description_full: Ennis, Inc. produces and sells business forms and other printed products in the United States. The company sells snap sets, continuous forms, laser cut sheets, tags, labels, envelopes, integrated products, jumbo rolls, and pressure sensitive products under the Ennis, Royal Business Forms, Block Graphics, ColorWorx, Enfusion, Uncompromised Check Solutions, VersaSeal, Ad Concepts, FormSource Limited, Star Award Ribbon Company, Witt Printing, Genforms, PrintGraphics, Calibrated Forms, PrintXcel, Printegra, Forms Manufacturers, Mutual Graphics, TRI-C Business Forms, Major Business Systems, Independent Printing, Hayes Graphics, Wright Business Graphics, Wright 360, Integrated Print & Graphics, the Flesh Company, AmeriPrint, Stylecraft, UMC Print, Eagle Graphics, Diamond Graphics, and Printing Technologies labels. It also offers point of purchase advertising under the Adams McClure brand; presentation and document folders under the Admore, Folder Express, and Independent Folders brands; custom printed products, labels, and custom and stock tags under the Ennis Tag & Label brand; custom and stock tags and labels under the Allen-Bailey Tag & Label, Atlas Tag & Label, Kay Toledo Tag, and Special Service Partners brands; custom and imprinted envelopes under the Trade Envelopes, Block Graphics, Wisco, and National Imprint Corporation brands; financial and security documents under the Northstar and General Financial Supply brands; and custom and stock pressure seal documents under the Infoseal and PrintXcel brands. In addition, it provides school photo marketing and national school forms for school portrait photographers and professional photo labs. The company distributes business forms and other business products through business forms distributors, resellers, direct mail, commercial printers, software companies, and advertising agencies. The company was formerly known as Ennis Business Forms, Inc. Ennis, Inc. was founded in 1909 and is headquartered in Midlothian, Texas.

financial_summary: Ennis, Inc. is a small-cap industrials business with a $528M market cap on $392M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -3% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 16% against a 7% cost of capital, a 9-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 29%.

The business throws off $41M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.24× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.
Management returns a meaningful 7.6% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 3.1% of the shares.

sect: Its 13% operating margin is roughly in line with the Industrials median (9%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.22x).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 38% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 10% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 21% and a beta of 0.47, it is more defensive than the market.
About $3.4M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 35% in the 2020 crash, 13% in the 2022 bear market and 64% in 2008.
val: The stock trades only 12% below its DCF fair value of $23.71, a thin margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 7%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $19.14 to $30.74 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/E 13.6 vs 23.3, EV/EBITDA 6.9 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 12.9 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 54% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 7.8% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 10.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The Street target $24.00 on average, 15% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 16% clears the cost of capital of 7.1% by 9pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.66).
It runs a 29% gross margin and converts 10% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.24x.
ROE of 14% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.6% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $27.7M.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 9.3, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at -3.1% over 3 years, 1.9% over 5 years and 1.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded -3.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 3.0% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 12, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has missed earnings estimates by 6.8% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 3.1%, and institutions hold 87%.
It returns 7.6% a year to shareholders (2.7% in buybacks and 5.0% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 2.0% a year over the last five.
people: With about 1,835 employees, each generates about $214K of revenue, 0.6x the Industrials median.
That works out to $22K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.2M (10x revenue per employee).
